note.headline: Tesla touches the top of its own valuation history while cash flow shrinks
note.happening: TSLA closed at 397.45, up 1.69% on the day. That is just under the top of its own-history valuation range (399.81) and below resistance at 408.62–417.44. The Verge reported that Cybertruck fans are turning on Elon Musk after he 'pulls the plug'; the headline does not say exactly what was stopped. The next earnings report is due on 2027-01-27.
note.business: Several numbers point to a weaker business. Sales growth in the latest quarter was -0.17% from a year earlier, compared with 15.78% two quarters ago. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, fell from 4.74% to 3.35%. Trailing free cash flow, the cash left after investment, fell from 6.8B to 3.3B. The filings also flag a demand warning: inventory is up 15% while latest-quarter sales are up 0%. Unsold cars can lead to price cuts and thinner margins. The balance sheet is not at risk. Tesla has 17.9B in cash, 8.0B in debt, 37.5B in net cash and 45.4B in total liquidity. Dilution (new shares diluting existing owners) is small at 0.43% a year. The Cybertruck report mainly affects sentiment and brand loyalty for now. Our data has no segment breakdown, so we cannot measure how much that product matters to revenue. A single product decision is a smaller issue than flat total sales and shrinking cash flow (general knowledge).
note.worth: The two valuation methods give very different answers. A discounted cash flow model values the company today based on the cash it should produce in future. Starting from 3.3B of trailing free cash flow, it gives 20.23 (bear), 25.02 (base) and 45.34 (bull) per share. Even with a 30% starting growth rate, the value is only 45.55. The filings estimate that the price needs about 51% a year growth, compared with 3% a year delivered over three years. The other method asks what Tesla is worth if investors keep paying the same price-to-sales multiple they have paid over the last five years. That gives 203.8 (low), 293.94 (mid) and 399.81 (high). Today's price-to-sales of 15.2 sits at the 77th percentile of its own 5-year history. The trailing P/E is 437.3. The whole gap comes down to one assumption: does the market keep valuing Tesla on sales and its story, or on the cash it actually produces? Even on the generous method, 397.45 is near the top.
bull: The balance sheet is strong: net cash of 37.5B and liquidity of 45.4B give room to invest through a slow patch.
The valuation inputs include analysts' next-year EPS growth of 25%. If that happens, the growth gap narrows.
The price is above its 50-day average (374.46) and 200-day average (382.86), and is still inside its own-history valuation range that tops out at 399.81.
bear: The price needs about 51% a year growth, compared with 3% a year delivered over 3 years and 8.3% over the last 12 months.

note.headline: Amazon edges just above its value range while cash burn keeps the case on hold
note.happening: Amazon closed at 267.44, up 0.48% on the day. That is just above the top of its value range of 187.93–266.17. The only relevant news is a reported Microsoft outage in which AWS and Google users also reported issues (CNBC). No earnings date is in the data, and the latest quarterly filing came on 2026-10-30.
note.business: Some things are changing the business itself. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 13.09% from 11.02%. That is real progress. Cash is going the other way. Free cash flow (cash left after running the business and investing in it) was -46.9B over the last 12 months, down from 10.6B a year earlier, a margin of -5.88%. Net debt (debt minus cash) is 66.7B, against total debt of 180.9B and cash of 55.8B. Growth is slowing. Sales rose 12.09% from a year earlier in the latest quarter, down from 16.61% two quarters ago. Filings also show unpaid customer bills up 61% while sales rose 12%. That can mean sales were pulled forward or customers are paying more slowly. Heavy investment spending is the likely cause of the cash burn (general knowledge), but our data has no segment detail to confirm it. Other things move only sentiment. The reported AWS outage is a headline. Nothing in the data shows lost demand from it. Liquidity, the cash and credit Amazon can draw on, is 114.2B, so its ability to fund itself is not at risk. What is at risk is the market's patience with spending that does not yet return cash.
note.worth: No discounted-cash-flow value is possible here, because free cash flow is negative. That leaves one method: Amazon's own price-to-sales history. Price-to-sales compares the company's market value with its yearly revenue. Amazon's ratio sat at its 20th, 50th and 80th percentile of the past five years at 187.93, 238.65 and 266.17 per share. Today's 3.6 times sales is at the 80th percentile, and the price of 267.44 is just above the top of that range. Against peers the stock looks cheap. The peer median is 6.7 times sales, and the growth-adjusted ratio is 0.61 of peers. The gap between the two views comes down to one question: should Amazon be valued against its own past or against faster-valued peers like MSFT and GOOGL? On earnings, the stock trades at 21.7 times trailing profit and 20.9 times this year's estimate. On next year's estimate it is 25.1 times, because analysts expect earnings per share to fall to 10.67 from 12.8. Filings also note that the price implies about 34% a year growth, while Amazon delivered 13% a year over 3 years.

events.title: PPI (producer prices)
events.line: Treat the morning print as a question and the close as the answer: QQQ's 200-day average at 680.94 decides whether to cut, and SPY's 50-day average at 764.43 decides whether to add, while history says most PPI days end up ordinary.

note.headline: PPI after a 1.34% September jump: QQQ's 200-day line at 680.94 is the test

lines.label: history
lines.text: Since 2016-11-16 there have been 125 PPI days. On a typical one, QQQ moved 0.68% in either direction, about the same as a normal day (0.7%, or 1.0x). SPY moved 0.56% against a normal 0.5% (1.1x). PPI days have usually been ordinary days.

lines.label: history
lines.text: QQQ closed up on 54% of PPI days and SPY on 55%. Big moves came on 20% of them for QQQ (beyond 1.57%) and 24% for SPY (beyond 1.13%).

lines.label: history
lines.text: The worst reaction was 2020-03-12, when QQQ fell 9.17% and SPY fell 9.57%. The best was QQQ +3.38% on 2026-06-11 and SPY +2.2% on 2022-03-15.

lines.label: history
lines.text: Producer prices rose 1.34% in September, the biggest of the last six months. The prior months were 1.08 (Apr), 0.52 (May), -0.12 (Jun), 0.15 (Jul) and 0.47 (Aug). The 3-month average is 0.65%, the 6-month average is 0.57%, and prices are up 6.35% from a year ago.

lines.label: history
lines.text: These figures have limits. No consensus forecast is available, so 'hot' and 'cool' below are measured against recent readings. The reaction history is close-to-close and is not split by whether the number surprised.

lines.label: judgment
lines.text: The latest reading is the hottest in six months and inflation is high from a year ago, so the market goes in already worried about prices. A second strong reading would confirm that worry rather than shock it.

lines.label: judgment
lines.text: QQQ closed at 688.17 in a sideways trend. It is 1.1% above its 200-day average (680.94), so the long trend holds, but 4.4% below its 50-day average (718.46), so the short trend is broken. It is down 5.47% over 20 days but up 6.35% over 5 days, a bounce from the 1-month low of 647.05 on Nov 5.

lines.label: judgment
lines.text: SPY closed at 757.12 and is in better shape. It is 1.0% below its 50-day average (764.43) and 3.7% above its 200-day average (728.99), with the 1-month low at 733.0 and the 1-month high at 773.09.

lines.label: judgment
lines.text: Fear is normal: the VIX was 17.49 on Nov 11, down from 19.46. That reading is stale; Nov 12 isn't stored yet. The market gate is inactive. Nothing in the setup points to a panic, but QQQ has little room above its long-term line.

plans.label: judgment
plans.if: The monthly change comes in above the 3-month average of 0.65%, especially a repeat near September's 1.34% or April's 1.08%.
plans.then: The market would likely read this as producer prices speeding up again. Rate-sensitive tech usually takes that hardest (general knowledge), so QQQ is more exposed than SPY. Add nothing on the day and let the close decide. If QQQ closes below 680.94, the long-term trend turns down: trim QQQ exposure. If SPY closes below 733.0, its decline is continuing. The plan is wrong if QQQ holds above 680.94 and SPY above 733.0 at the close despite the hot print. That would mean the number was already priced in, and existing exposure stays.

plans.label: judgment
plans.if: The monthly change lands between August's 0.47% and the 3-month average of 0.65%, around the 6-month average of 0.57%.
plans.then: The market would likely read this as no new information and go back to its sideways trend. Hold exposure unchanged. New QQQ exposure waits for a close above the 50-day average (718.46), and new SPY exposure for a close above 764.43. The plan is wrong if QQQ closes below 680.94 anyway, which would show the weakness is not about PPI. In that case trim as in the hot case.

plans.label: judgment
plans.if: The monthly change comes in below August's 0.47%. A reading at or under July's 0.15%, or negative like June's -0.12%, clearly counts.
plans.then: The market would likely read this as relief: September's jump looking like a one-off, which eases rate worries (general knowledge). SPY is closest to repair. A close above 764.43 puts its short-term trend back up and is the level to add on, with 773.09 (1-month high) as the full-recovery mark. QQQ needs a close above 718.46 to confirm, with 728.0 beyond that. The plan is wrong if the early relief fades and QQQ closes back below 680.94. Then the cool number did not change the trend: cut back any adds.

note.bottom_line: Treat the morning print as a question and the close as the answer: QQQ's 200-day average at 680.94 decides whether to cut, and SPY's 50-day average at 764.43 decides whether to add, while history says most PPI days end up ordinary.
